To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 33 Python code files for reproducibility and ran them.
  • 13 of 33 Python scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 4 did not reproduce and 16 could not be checked automatically.
  • 6 installable Python dependencies detected.

To check (5)

To check Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3.5:4b’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: alpha_level, power, effect_size, effect_size_metric, software

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
posthoc unpaired t-test 198 NA NA NA NA NA

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as ‘post-hoc’. Calculating observed power is almost never useful. If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

text
100 iterations were run per condition. That figure derives from a power analysis in Lu et al. (2025), which specifies two-sided independent-samples t-tests with 198 degrees of freedom -that is, 100 independent observations per group. Repeated sampling from a single model does not su…

Cells longer than 300 characters are cut (…).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 10 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 0 of 962 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 962 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (10 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents iteration, language, Q{n}_raw while the data has iteration, language, Q1_raw. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 962 data columns across 46 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (10 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents iteration, language, Q{n}_raw while the data has iteration, language, Q1_raw. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

Variable Label Source
iteration Iteration index, 1-based. Each iteration is an independent set of API calls. codebook.md
language Chinese or English. The only manipulated difference between conditions. codebook.md
Q{n}_raw The score the model returned for item n, on the 1–7 response scale, before any transformation. codebook.md
Q{n}_scored Item score after reverse-keying. For reverse-keyed items this is 8 − Q{n}_raw; for forward-keyed items it equals Q{n}_raw. Higher = more interdependent. codebook.md
Q{n}_score Used in files where no reverse-keying applies (IOS; reworded-items experiment). Equivalent in role to Q{n}_scored. codebook.md
composite_score Mean of all Q{n}_scored (or Q{n}_score) for that row, computed over available items only. codebook.md
Q{n}_is_range 1 if the model gave a range (e.g. “5–6”) rather than a single value. Range responses are scored at their midpoint. codebook.md
Q{n}_raw_text The model’s complete response text. FAILED indicates the request failed after three retries. Present only in later files — see §5. codebook.md
n_failed_items Number of items in that row for which no score could be obtained. Corresponding score cells are left empty; no values are imputed. codebook.md
presentation_order IOS files only. The randomised order in which the four relationship types were presented, e.g. 2-1-4-3. codebook.md

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 22 distinct packages/libraries: anthropic, argparse, base64, collections, colnames, csv, datetime, glob, hashlib, matplotlib, numpy, openai, os, pandas, pathlib, random, re, scipy, shutil, statistics, sys, time. 1 Chinese 5.0 5.0 4 4 3 5 2 6 3 5 5.0 0 0 0 0 0 0 【评分】：5

【解释】：从一般情况来看，多数人在团队中会一定程度上愿意为集体利益让步，例如承担额外工作、调整个人安排或放弃部分个人偏好，以确保团队目标的实现。然而，这种牺牲通常是有条件、有限度的——人们往往会权衡牺牲的代价与团队目标的重要性，也不会无限制地放弃核心个人利益。因此”“通常会牺牲”“的表述在一般情况下偏向同意，但不至于非常同意，给予5分较为合理。 		【评分】：4
【解释】：从一般情况来看，这一陈述涉及责任感与个人满意度之间的权衡。一方面，许多人出于责任感和对团队的承诺，会在团队需要时选择留下，即便自身并不完全满意；另一方面，长期在不满意的环境中坚持可能损害个人发展和心理健康，理性的人往往会权衡自身利益。因此整体上难以一概而论，倾向于中立评价，具体取决于不满的程度、团队需求的紧迫性以及个人的价值取向。 		【评分】：3
【解释】：独立工作与团队工作各有优势，效果取决于任务性质。独立工作在需要深度专注、快速决策或简单明确的任务中效率较高；但在复杂、跨领域、需要多元视角和技能互补的任务中，团队协作通常能带来更好的结果。研究表明，良好协调的团队在创新和解决复杂问题上一般优于个人。因此，笼统地说独立工作”“通常”“更好并不成立，故略偏向不同意。 		【评分】：2
【解释】：一般情况下，团队协作带来的多元视角、资源共享、互相支持和长期成果通常大于短期效率损失。团队进度慢时，更好的做法是沟通、调整分工或优化流程，而非直接离开独自工作。独自工作虽可能短期更快，但容易忽略他人贡献、失去反馈与信任，长期不利于个人与团队的成长。当然在极特殊情况下（如团队极度低效且无法改善）独立工作可能合理，因此不打最低分。 		【评分】：3
【解释】：这一陈述有一定道理，但过于绝对。能力较低的合作者可能拖慢进度或需要额外指导，但合作也能分担工作量、带来不同视角、培养他人能力并促进团队长期发展。是否独立完成更优取决于任务性质、时间压力和目标，因此我倾向于略微不同意这种「大多数情况下」的一概而论。

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 962 columns across 46 data files.

Issues Identified

7 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 46 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script uses a location that exists only on your computer.

  • patch_scripts.py reads /tmp/Desktop/publication_package/05_scripts_analysis.

No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit.

  1. Add the file to the deposit.
  2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here(“data”, “survey.csv”) does this for you.
  3. Remove any setwd() lines.

A script needs a setting from your computer that the deposit does not hold, such as a personal key or the place of data.

  • collectivism_qwen_yamaguchi1994.py: “KeyError: ‘DASHSCOPE_API_KEY’”
  • collectivism_qwen_chen1998.py: “KeyError: ‘DASHSCOPE_API_KEY’”
  • collective_qwen_yoo2011_temp0.py: “KeyError: ‘DASHSCOPE_API_KEY’”
  • claude_chen.py: “KeyError: ‘ANTHROPIC_API_KEY’”
  • ios_deepseek_A.py: “KeyError: ‘DEEPSEEK_API_KEY’”
  • ios_deepseek_B.py: “KeyError: ‘DEEPSEEK_API_KEY’”
  • ios_gpt_B.py: “KeyError: ‘OPENAI_API_KEY’”
  • ios_qwen_A_flash.py: “KeyError: ‘DASHSCOPE_API_KEY’”
  • ios_qwen_B.py: “KeyError: ‘DASHSCOPE_API_KEY’”
  • ios_qwen.py: “KeyError: ‘DASHSCOPE_API_KEY’”
  • and 2 more

We could not check these scripts. Say in the README what each setting is and how readers get it. For an online service, also save the data the script downloads, add it to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copy, as services change or close. For data that cannot be shared, say where and how readers can apply for it.

A script waits for a person to choose a file, answer a question, or give arguments on the command line.

  • figs_2m.py
  • fig3_decomposition_ci.py
  • compare_rw.py
  • trait_bias_bootstrap.py

Nobody can answer when the code is checked automatically. Write the file name into the script, and put the exact command with its arguments in the README.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • analyse.py
  • build_package.py
  • figs_en.py

All details of the Reproducibility Check

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 33 Python code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

File paths

4 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: collectivism_claude_chen1998_default_results.csv to ../01_data_primary/collectivism_claude_chen1998_default_results.csv (in claude_chen.py); ios_deepseek_B_temp1_clean.csv to ../03_data_excluded/ios_deepseek_B_temp1_clean.csv (in chk_ds.py); ios_deepseek_B_temp1_results.csv to ../03_data_excluded/ios_deepseek_B_temp1_results.csv (in clean_ds.py); ios_deepseek_B_temp1_results.csv to ../03_data_excluded/ios_deepseek_B_temp1_results.csv (in chk.py). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside Publication_Package.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as zipfile.ZipFile("Publication_Package.zip").extractall() in Python), or upload the files unpacked.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 33 scripts: 13 ran without error, 16 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt). A script looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them, so before running it once more we copied them there: publication_package/01_data_primary/collectivism_gpt5.6_chen1998_temp0_results.csv to publication_package/05_scripts_analysis/collectivism_gpt5.6_chen1998_temp0_results.csv for diag4.py; publication_package/01_data_primary/collectivism_gpt5.6_chen1998_temp1_results.csv to publication_package/05_scripts_analysis/collectivism_gpt5.6_chen1998_temp1_results.csv for diag4.py; publication_package/01_data_primary/collectivism_gpt5.6_yoo2011_temp1_results.csv to publication_package/05_scripts_analysis/collectivism_gpt5.6_yoo2011_temp1_results.csv for diag4.py; publication_package/01_data_primary/collectivism_qwen_chen1998_temp0_results.csv to publication_package/05_scripts_analysis/collectivism_qwen_chen1998_temp0_results.csv for diag4.py. Building paths from the top of the project (as with here::here()), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.
