Reverse-keyed items average +1.18; forward-keyed items average -0.05(Table 2). Pooling Yamaguchi and

Chen items across all four models gives +0.887 for reverse-keyed and -0.003 for forward-keyed items. In aggregate there is no language effect on forward-keyed items at all, and two of them (Q8, Q10) run in the opposite direction.

This pattern is consistent across all four models. Two American and two Chinese models, from four developers, using different architectures and alignment procedures, all show the composite difference resting on the same subset of items. It should be noted that this is not the simple conclusion that models handle negation differently across languages. Two of the five reverse-keyed Yamaguchi items show no effect at all -Q1 (+0.03) and Q5 (-0.20) -and both are negations; within reverse-keyed items the range runs from -0.20 to +3.01. This converges with Meyer et al. (2026), who excluded the negation explanation by a wholly different route.

4.3 Decomposition: two components with opposite signs

Decomposing responses into trait and bias components yields a highly regular pattern on the Yamaguchi scale (Figure 3). Table 3 Decomposition on the Yamaguchi scale. The rightmost column gives the cross-linguistic difference obtained from forward-keyed items alone, which equals Δθ + Δb. Model Temperature Δθ (trait) Δb (bias) |Δb| / |Δθ| Δθ + Δb (forward items only) GPT-5.6 0 +0.688 -0.780 1.13 -0.09 GPT-5.6 1 +0.558 -0.756 1.35 -0.20 Claude Default (run 1) +0.735 -0.355 0.48 +0.38 Claude default (run 2) +0.746 -0.346 0.46 +0.40 DeepSeek 0 +0.355 -0.447 1.26 -0.09 DeepSeek 1 +0.469 -0.477 1.02 -0.01 Qwen 0 +0.473 -0.873 1.85 -0.40 Qwen 1 +0.495 -0.911 1.84 -0.42 Mean +0.565 -0.618 -0.05

All eight estimates show a higher trait estimate and a lower bias estimate under Chinese prompting. The directional consistency of the bias component is as complete as that of the trait component, and its magnitude exceeds the trait component in five of the eight conditions, approaching a factor of two in Qwen. The two components do not order the models in the same way: the trait difference is largest in Claude (+0.74), the bias difference in Qwen (-0.91).

The bias component is a content-independent tendency to respond in one direction: positive values indicate a tendency to agree, whatever the item asks. The substance of this result is therefore that a model's tendency to agree is systematically stronger under English prompting than under Chinese prompting, by an amount comparable to, and often larger than, the putative cultural tendency.

Table 4 shows what this decomposition looks like for a single model, taking gpt-5.6 at temperature 0 as an example. The English condition is the telling one. The raw means for forward-keyed and reverse-keyed items are 5.54 and 5.33, both on the agreeing side of the scale. The model, that is, tends to endorse collectivist statements (such as "I stick with my group even through difficulties") and also the statements that contradict them (such as "I don't sacrifice self-interest for my group"). The two kinds of item are barely distinguished; the trait estimate accordingly sits close to the scale midpoint (4.11), while the bias estimate reaches 1.44. Under

Chinese prompting the two kinds of item separate clearly (5.45 and 3.86), the trait estimate rises to 4.80, and the bias falls to 0.66. Responding in the two languages therefore differs not only in the level of collectivist orientation but also in a tendency to agree that is independent of item content; the cross-linguistic difference in that tendency (0.78) is of roughly the same size as the difference in collectivist orientation (0.69).

Table 4 Decomposition for gpt-5.6 on the Yamaguchi scale (temperature 0) Language Forward mean Rf Reverse mean Rr composite 𝜽 " (trait) 𝒃 " (bias) Chinese 5.45 3.86 4.80 4.80 0.66 English 5.54 5.33 4.11 4.11 1.44 Difference (Chinese -English) -0.09 -1.47 +0.69 +0.69 -0.78 Note: forward and reverse means are raw scores, before reverse-keying. The composite is the mean of transformed scores. Sevenpoint scale, midpoint m = 4.

This component has not previously been reported for a structural reason: on a balanced scale the mean of transformed scores is algebraically identical to θw , and the bias cancels (compare the composite and θw columns of Table 4). Our recomputation confirms the identity -the mean composite effect on Yamaguchi is 0.565 and the mean Δθ from the decomposition is likewise 0.565. So long as analysis remains at the composite level, the bias component is invisible.

The decomposition on the Chen scale does not show the same regularity: Δb is positive in three conditions and negative in four, with a mean of -0.091. We attribute this to estimation precision rather than to a substantive counter-example. Chen has only five items (two forward, three reverse), so that the forward-item mean rests on two items alone; with these it must estimate two parameters, and its estimates are necessarily far noisier than Yamaguchi's five-and-five. A testable implication is that if this is noise, the between-iteration variability of b9 should be markedly larger on Chen than on Yamaguchi.

4.4 Implication: the limits of all-forward scales

The decomposition yields a testable prediction. On a balanced scale the composite equals θw and the bias component cancels; on an all-forward scale the composite equals θ + b and the two cannot be separated.

Section 4.3 showed that moving from English to Chinese raises the trait and lowers the bias (Δθ positive, Δb negative). On an all-forward scale, therefore, the two changes should offset one another, and the crosslinguistic effect observed should be smaller than on a balanced scale. Note: Values are means across eight estimates from four models. The first two bars compare within one scale, the first and third between scales.

We test this prediction in two ways (Figure 4). The first is a comparison between scales: the mean composite effect is 0.565 on the Yamaguchi scale, which is balanced, and 0.228 on the Yoo scale, which is all-forwardless than half. The second is a comparison within a scale. The five forward-keyed Yamaguchi items constitute an all-forward instrument in their own right, and the cross-linguistic difference in their mean is exactly Δθ + Δb (Table 3, final column). On these five items alone, six of the eight estimates are negative, with a mean of -0.05, negligible on a seven-point scale; the two exceptions are Claude, whose bias difference is less than half its trait difference. For gpt-5.6 at temperature 0, a trait difference of +0.69 and a bias difference of -0.78 sum to -0.09: the same model, on the same scale, shows a clear language effect when all ten items are used and a near-zero effect of the opposite sign when only the five forward-keyed items are.

The two tests have complementary strengths and weaknesses. The between-scale comparison is empirically independent of the decomposition in §4.3 but confounds keying with item content: the smaller Yoo effect could in principle reflect its items rather than its keying. The within-scale comparison holds item content constant and so removes that confound, but it is not independent of the decomposition: the forward-item difference is algebraically equal to Δθ + Δb, and is therefore a consequence of the §4.3 result rather than an independent test of it. The first supplies independence, the second control; both point the same way.

Together the two results carry an implication beyond the observation that all-forward scales show smaller effects. The within-scale value also coincides with the mean forward-item difference reported in §4.2, and the decomposition explains it: the language effect vanishes on forward-keyed items not because they carry no trait difference, but because it is cancelled by a bias difference of opposite sign. On a scale with no reversekeyed items, trait and bias cannot in principle be separated; the composite carries both. The two all-forward instruments examined here -the Yamaguchi forward items and the Yoo scale -yield different values (-0.05 and 0.228), and this is precisely the difficulty: the relative size of the two components differs from one set of items to another, and no all-forward instrument can tell the researcher which combination it has measured.

The 0.228 reported on Yoo may be the residue of a trait effect partly cancelled by bias, or it may be largely bias itself; from that scale's data there is no way to tell. Meyer et al. (2026) corroborate this from another direction: across the 29 instruments they examine, the interitem consistency of model responses is almost entirely predicted by the proportion of reverse-keyed items (r = -0.95). In human research, item keying is a trade-off: Weijters and Baumgartner (2012) document both the benefits of reversed items and their costs, and advocate continued but cautious use. In cross-linguistic work on language models the trade-off no longer balanced. Whatever reversed items cost in reliability, without them the part of a cross-linguistic difference that belongs to the construct cannot be identified. A crosslinguistic difference reported on an all-forward scale therefore does not by itself support an inference about the construct -a limitation that has not previously been noted in work of this kind.

The largest effect in the original study (Lu et al., 2025) appears on the Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale (d = 1.67), which its authors single out as minimising linguistic confounds because "little or no translation of statements is required". Within the present framework this is not a counter-example but an illustration: the IOS carries no item keying at all, so trait and bias are entirely confounded on it and cannot be separated. The largest effect in that study thus comes from the instrument on which decomposition is least possible -and it is singled out precisely for the feature that makes decomposition impossible. We collected IOS data but do not report them here owing to incomplete coverage ( §6.1); decomposing that measure would require a purpose-built design and is a direction for further work.

4.5 Manipulation one: rewording

The evidence in § §4.2-4.3 is correlational: it shows that the effect covaries with certain items, not that their wording produces it. To test that, we reworded the five reverse-keyed Yamaguchi items as forward statements with the same propositional content and kept the five forward items verbatim as controls. All ten were administered to two models, gpt-5.6 and qwen-max, each alongside a baseline of the original items collected on the same day -100 iterations per language in every condition, with no failed items (Figure 5). The internal validity of the manipulation holds in both models. The five unchanged control items moved by +0.024 on average in gpt-5.6 and by +0.010 in qwen-max; nine of the ten item-level changes fell within ±0.09, the largest being +0.25 (Table 5). The collection process therefore introduces no appreciable variance. Against that baseline, the reworded items moved substantially in both models: from +1.454 to +0.352 in gpt-5.6, and from +0.600 to -0.093 in qwen-max.

The two models converge on the central point and diverge on the details. They converge in that rewording moved the reworded items by roughly a scale point in each and in that Q2 -the second largest contributor in both -fell to almost exactly zero (+0.01 in gpt-5.6, -0.01 in qwen). They diverge on Q6 and Q9. In gpt-5.6, Q6 fell by more than half (+3.24 → +1.43) and Q9 fell to zero (+1.02 → -0.01); in qwen-max, Q6 rose (+1.72 → +2.29) and Q9 overshot into reversal (+1.03 → -1.72). This divergence is informative rather than inconvenient.

With one model, the anomalous behaviour of Q6 could not be distinguished from noise or from a flaw in the rewording. With two, it is identifiable as a property of qwen-max: the same reworded item behaves as predicted in one model and against prediction in the other. The Q9 result admits the same reading. Our rewording of Q9 replaced an assertion of opposition with an expression of restraint, and we noted in advance that this might introduce a semantic component absent from the original. In gpt-5.

6 it did not -the effect simply vanished. In qwen-max it did. The experiment therefore supports a conclusion that does not depend on the model, and disconfirms one that does not survive either model. What is supported is that the cross-linguistic difference is driven by specific item wording: in two models from two vendors, rewording five items moved their mean difference by about a scale point while five unchanged items moved by less than 0.03. What is disconfirmed is that the driving mechanism is the grammatical feature of negation. Were it so, all five reworded items should have behaved alike within a model and alike across models; instead Q1 and Q5 barely moved in either, and Q6 moved in opposite directions in the two. This converges with §4.2 and with the negation test of Meyer et al. (2026), reached by a third route. If not grammar, then what? One possibility, which we raise without testing it, is that what matters is pragmatic rather than semantic equivalence. Back-translation establishes that two versions of an item mean the same thing; it does not establish that asserting them would be taken to be doing the same thing. Q6 is suggestive here. "I don't support my group when they are wrong" and 「当所在团队犯错时，我不会支持我所在的团 队」 are semantically equivalent and would pass a back-translation check, yet the English sentence might be heard as a refusal to endorse wrongdoing and the Chinese as a declaration of disloyalty. The models agree with it in English and disagree with it in Chinese. Whether that is because the two sentences perform different acts, we cannot say from these data.

Two things count against taking this further. The three items that carry the effect do all concern open opposition to one's group, which is consistent with the suggestion; but three items are too few to establish a regularity, and the two that carry no effect differ from them in more than one way. More importantly, the rewording results do not behave as a property of items would: the same reworded Q6 moved as predicted in gpt-5.6 and against prediction in qwen-max. Any account of this kind would therefore have to be stated per model, and we have two models.

The accurate statement is that item wording is the source of the cross-linguistic difference, that the magnitude of the difference is acutely sensitive to it, and that how a particular item responds to a particular rewording is a property of the model rather than of the item -whether of its grammatical class or of whatever else distinguishes it.

4.6 Manipulation two: stability of a model identifier

The same-day baselines were not part of the original design. They were added because a first comparison, using qwen-max data collected four weeks earlier as the baseline, produced an uninterpretable result: the five control items -not one word of which had been altered -moved by an average of +1.143, a mean signed change. Rewording cannot affect items that were not reworded, so the variance had another source.

Recollecting the original items on the day of the rewording resolved the anomaly, and revealed where the variance came from (Figure 6). Note: Annotated values mark changes exceeding one scale point.

The +1.143 cited in the text is a mean signed change across the five control items only.

Stability over four weeks differs between the two vendors by roughly an order of magnitude (Table 6). For gpt-5.6 the mean absolute change was 0.11 scale points, with no item moving by more than 0.31; the two collections are nearly indistinguishable. For qwen-max it was 0.97, with four of the ten items moving by more than one scale point: Q6 fell by 2.39 points and Q10 reversed sign, while Q3 and Q8 moved by +1.65 and +1.39.

That mean change is of the same order as the language effect this study reports (0.36 to 0.75), and in several items larger.

The comparison carries its own control in two directions. Within the pipeline, the rewording experiment established that repeating collection on the same day moves unchanged items by 0.010 in one model to 0.024 in the other. Between models, gpt-5.6 demonstrates that a four-week interval need not produce movement at all: the collection procedure, parsing rules and statistical treatment were identical for both models on both occasions. The 0.97 observed in qwen-max therefore cannot be attributed to the measurement process and must be attributed to the model.

Had only qwen-max been examined, the finding would have read as a general warning about model drift. The gpt-5.6 comparison shows that the warning is both more specific and harder to act on: whether a model identifier without a version snapshot denotes a reproducible condition depends on the vendor's deployment practice, and nothing in the identifier itself indicates which case one is in.

5 Discussion

5.1 What the cross-linguistic difference measures

The results point to different layers of the same conclusion. The difference is concentrated at the item level and absent on forward-keyed items. It comprises two separable components with opposite signs, one of which is unrelated to item content and comparable in magnitude. It is driven by item wording as two manipulations show. And the conditions under which any of it is measured are themselves unstable in one vendor and not the other. Together these indicate that the observed cross-linguistic difference is not a clean index of social orientation: it contains at least one component unrelated to the construct, and that component is identifiable only on scales with balanced keying.

This conclusion does not claim that language models lack culturally patterned responses, nor that the crosslinguistic difference reported by Lu et al.(2025) is spurious. The composite effect is real and replicable. What it claims is that the inference from a composite difference to a cultural orientation requires an assumption of item and keying equivalence that these data do not support. Meyer et al. (2026) show that differences between models are driven mainly by bias rather than trait; in their framework, bias is a respondent-level parameter. Applying the same decomposition to language conditions within a single model, we find that bias does not belong to the model alone: in all eight balanced-keying conditions, the same model shows higher bias under English prompting than under Chinese. Bias is, at least in part, a property of model and prompt language jointly. Meyer et al. found bias to be two-sided across models -some models leaning towards agreement, others away from it -and on that basis excluded simple acquiescence. The language effect observed here is, by contrast, uniform in direction: English prompting raised the tendency to agree in every condition. The two findings are about different things. Meyer et al. compares levels of bias between models; we compare change in bias within a model as language varies. A monolingual design cannot observe the second, which is why the uniformity we find is not in tension with the two-sideness they report.

5.2 Relation to existing work

What Braun (2025) reports is a preference for the response token itself: models lean towards "no" whether it signals agreement or disagreement. The bias measured here is a preference for one pole of a rating scale, independent of item content. Both are response biases, but they operate at different levels: one over answer tokens; the other over position on a rating scale. The present finding is that the magnitude of the latter varies with the language of the prompt.

Meyer et al. and the present study also converge by different routes on a secondary conclusion: the reversekeying effect cannot be attributed to negation. They excluded it by restricting analysis to negation-free reverse-keyed items; we exclude it through the rewording experiment and the item-level heterogeneity. The relation to cross-cultural psychology is more direct. Measurement invariance is a precondition for crosscultural comparison in human research, with established methods for testing it. In essence, this study performs a minimal version of that check on language models, and the premise of equivalence does not survive it.

5.3 An assumption the data do not satisfy

A limitation of the decomposition framework itself should be stated. It assumes that bias does not vary with item content: for a given respondent, b enters every item identically. Our item-level data do not satisfy this assumption: among the five reverse-keyed Yamaguchi items, cross-linguistic differences range from -0.20 to +3.01.

θw and bw should therefore be understood here as two orthogonal summaries of the response pattern rather than as clean recoveries of latent parameters. There is an item × language interaction the model does not contain, and this is not a peculiarity of the present data. Kriegmair and Wulff (2026) use crossed randomeffects models to partition the variance of model responses into consensus, a model-level bias, a model × stimulus interaction and residual, and report that the interaction averages 16.9% -evidence that stimulusspecific individuality in models is real and substantial, not an artefact of response bias or noise. Proper treatment of the present data would require the same approach, or differential item functioning analysis; extending it to a cross-linguistic design, so as to estimate the item × language interaction directly, is a clear direction for further work.

The limitation does not weaken the central conclusion but points in the same direction: if the bias component already shows so regular a cross-linguistic pattern under a parsimonious model that omits item interactions, the picture under a fuller model will be more complicated, not less.

5.4 Practical implications

For users: addressing a model in Chinese rather than English changes the orientation expressed in its answers, and the four models examined here differ in the size of that change. For anyone seeking guidance in a highstakes domain, the language of the query is a variable, and it is not one most users know they are setting.

For researchers, the results point to three checks. What they have in common is that each rules out a situation in which the data look interpretable but are not.

First, cross-linguistic comparison should use scales with balanced keying. On an instrument with no reversekeyed items, trait and bias are not separable in principle, and an observed difference carries both. This is a problem of identification, not of precision: no number of iterations and no refinement of the statistics can repair it. Two values from a single scale show the consequence ( §4.4): 0.565 across all ten items, and -0.05 on its five forward-keyed items alone.

Second, composite analysis should always be accompanied by item-level decomposition. Averaging over items of opposite sign returns a number that describes none of them. In this study a composite difference of 0.565 concealed item differences ranging from -0.91 to +3.01 (Table 2); without decomposition, a researcher cannot tell whether a reported effect is distributed across the items or carried by two or three of them. The first supports an inference about the construct and the second does not, and the composite is silent on which it is.

Third, comparison across time requires a contemporaneous control. This is the least intuitive of the three and the least dispensable on the present evidence. Of the two models examined, one was stable to a tenth of a scale point over four weeks while the other moved by 0.97 on average -the same order as the effect being measured -and there was no way to tell in advance which was which. The identifier gives no indication: both collections used the same identifier, the same parameters and the same script. A contemporaneous control costs one additional collection; its absence can cost the interpretability of an entire comparison.

None of the three requires new instruments or new theory; what they require is that the check be performed before the comparison rather than after it is questioned.

6 Limitations

The limitations fall into three kinds: what the design covers, how precisely the decomposition can be estimated, and what the inferential statistics can and cannot support.

6.1 Design and coverage

Four models span two development contexts, which is enough to show that the effect is not confined to one of them, but not enough to attribute any difference in magnitude to that contrast. Developer origin is confounded with architecture, corpus, alignment procedure and release date.

The analysis requires instruments with reverse-keyed items, which confines it to the three Likert measures of social orientation. Vignette ratings, logical judgements and probability estimates carry no keying, so neither the decomposition nor the rewording manipulation applies to them; they were not administered. The Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale was collected but is not reported: it requires a vision-capable model, each developer's vision model differs from its flagship text model, and only two of the four were completed. Those data are deposited with the rest. What is reported here is therefore a test of the social orientation measures only. Whether the same decomposition applies to the cognitive style tasks -where no keying exists to exploit -remains unknown.

Claude was administered the Chen scale at 52 iterations rather than 100, at the API default temperature, and through a different API account from that used for its other scales; these deviations arose from credit exhaustion during collection. The result is reported as a separate line in all tables and is not pooled with the conditions collected at two temperatures. Qwen fell short of 100 iterations on two scales (96-99). Given the documented stability of estimates, these are unlikely to affect the conclusions, but are reported rather than concealed.

6.2 Precision of the decomposition

The Chen scale has only five items (two forward, three reverse) with which to estimate two parameters. The decomposition is identified, but the forward-item mean rests on two items, and the estimates are correspondingly noisy. They are therefore reported as secondary evidence of limited precision; the primary evidence comes from Yamaguchi, which is perfectly balanced and twice as long. The Yoo scale has a keying proportion of zero and cannot be decomposed; our claim about that scale is accordingly a negative one -that its effect cannot be read as a construct difference -rather than an estimate of its components.

6.3 Coverage of the two manipulations

Both manipulations were run on two models and on one scale of the three. The models were chosen to span the two development contexts represented in the main analysis, but two observations cannot characterise a distribution, and neither Claude nor DeepSeek was examined. Whether the divergence on Q6 marks qwenmax as unusual, or gpt-5.6 as unusual, cannot be settled from two cases.

The rewording manipulation altered five items, of which only three had carried an appreciable effect. Three observations per model suffice to disconfirm a universal claim about negation but fall short of establishing an alternative mechanism. Extending the manipulation to the three reverse-keyed Chen items and to two further models would require roughly the same number of API calls as a single cell of the main analysis.

Rewording is not itself a neutral operation. The Q9 result shows that removing a confrontational sense may introduce a component of restraint, and that whether this happens depends on the model: the same reworded item behaved as intended in gpt-5.6 and did not in qwen-max. An ideal rewording would hold propositional content strictly constant while changing only the syntactic frame; for items carrying ethical or loyalty connotations this requirement may be unsatisfiable in principle -a difficulty that is perhaps itself part of the phenomenon. Independent bilingual ratings of the semantic equivalence of each rewording would strengthen any extension of this design.

The drift comparison rests on two time points in each model, and so cannot characterise the shape of drift: whether it is gradual or stepwise, whether it coincides with an announced release, and whether the interval between collections matters.

Its directional conclusion does not depend on breadth of coverage -one clear instance is enough to disconfirm the assumption that an identifier without a version snapshot constitutes a reproducible condition -but the practical question of how often to expect such a change remains open.

6.4 Statistical inference and instruments

The inferential statistics rest on an independence assumption that repeated sampling from a single model does not satisfy; the p values reported are uniformly small, but their smallness is a property of the denominator. Cohen's 𝒹 ranged from 1.01 to 8.09 across our conditions, where standard deviations fell between 0.000 and 0.255 -the denominator here captures a model's sampling stochasticity, not variation between respondents. The consequence is not only inflation but reordering: DeepSeek shows the smallest raw difference of the four (0.355) yet the second largest 𝒹 (5.05), because its responses are the most deterministic.

Such effect sizes are comparable neither across models nor with the human literature from which the conventional benchmarks derive.

Items were used verbatim rather than reworded to guard against memorisation of published instruments; the possibility that models encountered these scales in training cannot be excluded. The rewording experiment partly mitigates this concern -reworded items cannot have been memorised, yet they still produced systematic cross-linguistic differences -but its coverage is too narrow to exclude a memorisation account entirely.

Finally, the analysis is confined to two languages and one construct domain. Whether the same decomposition pattern appears in other language pairs, or in other constructs measured with reverse-keyed items, is unknown and worth establishing before the present conclusion is generalised.

7 Conclusion

At the composite level the difference is real: responses are more interdependent under Chinese prompting than under English. But a composite is a mean, and means conceal. Three of the ten items carry almost the whole effect, and four models from different developers, built on different architectures, rest their difference on the same three. The difference itself proves to be not one quantity but two: a difference in the construct the instrument is meant to measure, and a difference in directional response bias -how far a model leans towards one end of the scale whatever it is asked. Moving from English to Chinese raised the construct difference and lowered the tendency to agree in every balanced-keying condition. Under English prompting, models endorse both "I stick with my group even through difficulties" and the statement that contradicts itnot occasionally, but on average.

That the two components can be separated only on instruments containing reverse-keyed items is a property of the measurement model. What this study adds is that in the cross-linguistic case they run in opposite directions. That is why, on an instrument without reverse-keyed items, they offset and the value obtained is neither trait nor bias but what remains once the two have cancelled. A difference reported on such an instrument does not establish that models differ in the construct, only that they answered differently.

Two further manipulations bear on how far the finding can be pushed. The difference is produced by wording: altering five items moved their differences by about a scale point each while five untouched items barely moved.

But it is not produced by negation: two of the five negated items carried no effect to begin with and barely moved under rewording, and the same reworded item moved in opposite directions in the two models.

And the conditions under which any of this is measured are not guaranteed to hold: over four weeks, under the same identifier, one model moved by a tenth of a scale point and another by almost a full point.

What can be said now is this: any cross-linguistic comparison of models should include three checksbalanced keying, decomposition to the item level, and a contemporaneous control whenever collections are compared across time. None requires new instruments or new theory. What they require is that the check precede the comparison, rather than follow the objection.
